lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: What you said the other day to Odysseus about death, Achilles — I have to tell you, it was unworthy of you. Unworthy of both your teachers, Chiron and Phoenix. I was listening when you said you'd rather be a hired hand above ground, working for some landless nobody who can barely feed himself, than rule over every soul down here. That's the kind of thing a cowardly Phrygian might say — someone with an embarrassing attachment to breathing. But the son of Peleus? The most reckless hero who ever lived? To think so cheaply of yourself — it contradicts everything you actually did. You had the choice: a long, quiet reign in Phthia, no one the wiser. You chose death with glory instead. Voluntarily.
lines.note: Antilochus is not unkind — he's firm. He genuinely admires Achilles and finds the self-pity out of character. The speech is a corrective, not a rebuke.

lines.speaker: Achilles
lines.text: Son of Nestor — when I said that, I hadn't been here long. I didn't know which was better. I was still taken in by that wretched little notion of reputation, and I chose it over life. But I understand now. Glory is worthless, however much the poets up there recite it. Down here, everyone is equal. That beauty I had, Antilochus — [pause] gone. The strength — gone. We all lie in the same darkness, indistinguishable from each other. The dead Trojans don't fear me. The dead Achaeans don't wait on me. Perfect equality — the bad man and the good man are exactly the same corpse. That is what torments me. That is why I would rather be a farmhand and alive.
lines.note: This is the emotional center of the dialogue. Achilles is not performing grief — he means every word. No irony here.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: All the same — what can anyone do about it, Achilles? This is what nature decided: everyone dies, without exception. We have to keep the law and not be miserable about what's been ordained. Besides — look how many of your companions are here with you. Odysseus will show up soon enough, he always does. There's some comfort in sharing it, isn't there? In knowing you're not the only one it happened to. Look at Heracles — Meleager — all those extraordinary men. I don't think they'd accept an offer to go back up and hire themselves out to paupers with nothing to their names.
lines.note: Antilochus's consolation is practical and well-intentioned, but he knows it won't fully land. He's doing his best.

lines.speaker: Achilles
lines.text: That's what a friend would say. But I can't explain it — the memory of life just grieves me. And I think it grieves each of you too. If you won't admit it, that only makes it worse — suffering in silence and pretending otherwise.
lines.note: Achilles is not wrong, and he knows it. This is his slight advantage in the exchange.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: No — it makes us better, Achilles. Because we can see that saying so is pointless. We've decided to keep quiet and bear it and get on with things, rather than make ourselves look ridiculous — the way you're doing right now, making wishes that will never come true.
lines.note: The final line is gentle but it lands. Antilochus isn't cruel — but he gets the last word, and it's the right one. A beat of silence after it would not go amiss.
